x: Operational and mathematical value tree decompositions across five diagnostic lenses.
b: operational decomposition of financial performance across transport and logistics. financial metrics are the downstream consequence of repeating unit-of-work transactions. these five lenses break financial results into verifiable physical drivers. the exception lens the question: where does the deviation go? apply this when diagnosing any mechanism, not only the ones about exceptions. a value tree decomposes a metric into drivers, and each driver into a cost per unit of work times a volume of work. the lens splits that unit of work one level further, into the transactions that went to plan and the transactions that deviated, and then follows the deviation: who touches it? which function picks up a load that missed its appointment, a file with a document mismatch, an invoice the customer rejected. name the function, not the system. how many times is it touched? a deviation that returns to the same desk three times is three units of cost, not one. does the cost scale with volume, or with the deviation rate? this is the test that matters. a cost that scales with the deviation rate does not fall when volume grows, and it does not fall when the happy path is automated. why it matters for reading a mechanism. automation is usually applied to the path that goes to plan, because that path is specifiable. the deviating transactions keep their manual handling, so unit cost stops falling even though throughput rises. in the financials this reads as cost per unit of work resistant to volume scaling, and productivity metrics that plateau after an automation programme rather than during one. that plateau is the signature to look for — it is what separates a company that automated the transaction from one that automated the exception. what must be sourced, never assumed. the share of transactions that deviate and the share of operational attention they consume are company-specific and vary by operating model, lane, and customer. they are diagnostic questions, not constants. ask them; do not carry a ratio into a note. diagnostic question: "what share of your operations team's day goes to loads that did not go to plan?" named failure. the unit-of-work substitution anti-pattern the claim: "the value is worth x% of this cost line." treat a value pool sized as a percentage of a revenue or cost ratio as an anti-pattern, and go looking for the unit of work it replaced. a value tree ends in a cost per unit of work times a volume of work. when the unit of work is not established, the arithmetic has nowhere to land. the sizing then falls back on the only quantity available: a disclosed cost line multiplied by an estimated addressable share. the result looks like a value tree and carries a defensible-sounding baseline. it also cannot be reconstructed by the company from its own operating data, which is the test it fails. the signature is a sentence of the form "group g&a of $294.1m x 45% — our estimated transactional share" , or "1.5 to 3.0 margin points on 43% of segment revenue" . two things are true of every instance: the estimated share carries most of the value and none of the evidence. it is the number a cfo attacks first, correctly, because it is the only one in the chain that was not observed. a computable unit-of-work figure usually existed and was not used. this is the part that matters. the substitution is rarely necessary. the test: compute the unit cost and see which way it moved before accepting a cost-ratio pool, take the disclosed cost line, divide it by the disclosed volume of work, and compare two periods. three outcomes: unit cost rose while the ratio fell. the ratio was tracking revenue, not work. the pool is real but is probably on a different line than the one proposed. unit cost was flat. there is no unit-cost problem on that line, whatever the ratio did. sizing a pool there is sizing a number that did not move. unit cost fell. the line is improving and the ratio is a mix artefact. a pursuit document sized its largest pool as 45% of matson, inc. 's $294.1m general and administrative line. it named that share as its own estimate, and as the assumption worth testing first. the volume of work — containers carried, in feu — is disclosed, as is every major cost line. computing them: line 2025 per feu 2024 per feu change general and administrative $753 $757 −0.5% vessel operating expense $1,521 $1,522 −0.1% operating overhead $843 $820 +2.7% direct cargo expense $2,559 $2,444 +4.7% — of which the terminal jv $875 $800 +9.4% overhead as a ratio to revenue had risen from 5.8% to 8.5% since fy2021, which is what the document observed. cost per unit of work on that same line was flat. the line that deteriorated was terminal handling, and within it the joint-venture terminal operator — the one the document explicitly declined to build on, on the correct ground that the company does not control it. the finding is not that the document was careless. it reasoned from the ratio it could see to the conclusion the ratio supported. the unit cost was one division away and inverts the answer. why this is not the exception lens the exception lens asks where the deviation goes once the unit of work is established. this anti-pattern is upstream of it: the unit of work was never established, so there is nothing to split. run this test first; the exception lens is what you apply to whatever the unit turns out to be. how to write it where a unit of work is disclosed, size on it. where it is not, say the pool cannot be sized from outside, and name it as the first thing a diagnostic measures. matson, inc. does not publish deployed slot capacity, so load factor is not computable at all. that is a stronger position than a number resting on an estimated share, because it survives being checked. per, our inability to compute a unit cost is an observation of the disclosure, not a finding about the company. and per, a stated assumption does not license a figure the evidence cannot carry: the figure is what gets copied into

b: every measure used on this site, with the model it belongs to. a metric read against the wrong model is worse than no metric, because it looks like an answer. net revenue / adjusted gross profit (brokerage) definition: gross revenue less purchased transportation and related services why it matters: the only revenue line for a broker that reflects company performance rather than market rates moves up: buying capacity below the price sold; contract mix over spot in a falling market; spot exposure in a rising market moves down: manual load coverage forcing market-rate buys; customer mix shifting to low-margin contract freight where to find it: 10-k md&a, usually a named non-gaap reconciliation table. often absent from standard xbrl taxonomy — extract from filing text. reference: c.h. robinson fy2025: $2,729,410k, 16.8% of total revenue (10-k filed 2026-02-13) common misread: comparing across companies with different contract/spot mix diagnostic question: when a tender comes in at a rate below what you can buy that lane for today, who makes the cover-or-decline call, and what do they look at before they make it? adjusted operating margin (brokerage) definition: operating income ÷ adjusted gross profit why it matters: the company's own disclosed efficiency measure. using it signals you read the filing rather than a screener. moves up: headcount productivity gains; automation of load coverage moves down: personnel cost growth outpacing net revenue; acquisition integration overhead reference: c.h. robinson fy2025: 29.1% (operating income $794,961k ÷ adjusted gross profit $2,729,410k) common misread: confusing with gaap operating margin on gross revenue (4.9% for the same company, same year) diagnostic question: how many people touch a single load between the customer tender and the carrier invoice being paid, and what does each of them do to it? net revenue per load definition: net revenue ÷ loads handled why it matters: the cleanest single measure of pricing discipline moves up: dynamic pricing; better carrier sourcing; freight mix to harder-to-cover lanes moves down: manual sourcing at market rates; commoditised lane mix where to find it: load counts sometimes disclosed in md&a or investor decks; otherwise modelled common misread: ignoring lane mix. a falling number may be mix, not execution. diagnostic question: which lanes did your reps earn the most on last quarter, and how did they know to price those lanes that way? loads per rep per day definition: loads handled ÷ (customer-facing headcount × working days) why it matters: the productivity metric brokers manage to internally. using it signals operational fluency. moves up: automation of quoting, tendering, tracking, and check calls moves down: manual exception handling; fragmented systems post-acquisition where to find it: rarely disclosed. model from headcount and load counts, label. diagnostic question: what does a rep actually do between 7am and 9am, and which of those steps would disappear if your systems talked to each other? sg&a as % of net revenue (brokerage) definition: sg&a ÷ net revenue why it matters: for an asset-light business this is the cost structure moves up: headcount growth ahead of volume; integration overhead; duplicate systems moves down: automation; consolidation of acquired back offices common misread: computing against gross revenue, which makes every broker look efficient diagnostic question: of the back offices you have acquired, how many are still running their own process on their own system, and what has kept them there? operating ratio (asset carriage) definition: operating expenses ÷ revenue. often quoted ex-fuel-surcharge. why it matters: the standard measure for asset carriers. lower is better. moves up (worse): driver wage inflation; utilisation decline; insurance; empty miles moves down (better): density; utilisation; fuel efficiency common misread: comparing or across carriers without normalising for fuel surcharge treatment and length of haul diagnostic question: where do your empty miles come from - which lanes, which customers, and which planning decisions put them there?
